title: Wedding Dress Code for Men
metaTitle: Wedding Dress Code for Men: White Tie to Casual, Code by Code
metaDescription: Wedding dress code for men, code by code: tailcoat for white tie, tuxedo for black tie, dark suit for cocktail, blazer for dressy casual, khakis for casual.
h1: Wedding Dress Code for Men: What Every Invitation Wording Asks You to Wear
answer: Match the outfit to the code on the invitation. White tie: black tailcoat, white vest, white bow tie. Black tie: tuxedo with a black bow tie. Black tie optional or formal: tuxedo or dark suit and tie. Semi-formal or cocktail: dark suit and tie. Dressy casual: blazer and slacks, tie optional. Casual: khakis and a button-down or polo. No code? Wear a suit.
intro: A wedding dress code for men comes down to one question: which jacket? Tailcoat, tuxedo, dark suit, blazer or none. Once you know which of those the invitation asks for, everything else follows: the shirt, the tie and the shoes. The Emily Post Institute's attire guide lists men's clothing for every code from white tie to casual, and its wedding-guest guidance splits each level into daytime and evening. This page walks the whole ladder in order, so you can find your invitation's wording, see exactly what it asks for, and follow the link to the deeper guide for that code. It also covers the wordings that sit outside the ladder, like beach, festive and no code at all.

contentSections.content: Read across for your code. Each row is one invitation wording. The columns are the four choices that decide whether a man is dressed correctly. The jacket column changes at almost every step. The tie column changes only twice, from bow tie to necktie at black tie optional, and from required to optional at dressy casual. Most mistakes with a wedding dress code for men come down to wearing a jacket from the wrong row.

contentSections.heading: White tie: the rare top rung
contentSections.content:
White tie, also called full evening dress, is the most formal code there is. You are only likely to see it at state occasions, some very traditional balls, and the occasional grand evening wedding. Emily Post's men's list leaves no room for interpretation: a black tailcoat with matching trousers, a white piqué wing-collared shirt, braces, studs and cufflinks, a white vest, a white bow tie, white or gray gloves, black patent shoes and black dress socks. It also notes a transatlantic detail. The trousers carry one satin or braid stripe in the US, two in Europe and the UK.

A tuxedo is not white tie, and a white bow tie on a tuxedo does not turn it into white tie. Few men own tails, so for a white-tie wedding, rent from a formalwear specialist and allow time for a fitting. Tailcoats are cut to sit precisely at the waist, and off-the-rack sizing rarely gets it right.

contentSections.heading: Black tie attire for men
contentSections.content:
Black tie is the most common formal code at evening weddings, and the most precise. Emily Post's list: a black tuxedo jacket and matching trousers, a formal white pleated or piqué shirt, studs and cufflinks, a black bow tie, a black cummerbund or vest, optional dressy braces, no gloves, black patent shoes and black dress socks. Wikipedia's black tie article adds two useful details. Midnight blue is once again a popular alternative to black, and patent leather is more formal than matte, though a black lace-up oxford in polished calfskin is also accepted.

Three variations matter at weddings:
• Warm weather. In summer, in the tropics or on a cruise, Emily Post says a white dinner jacket with black tuxedo trousers and the rest of the black-tie wardrobe is appropriate.
• Creative black tie. Same tuxedo foundation, with room for a black shirt or a colored or patterned bow tie and cummerbund.
• Daytime. Black tie is an evening code. If an invitation says black tie for an afternoon ceremony, dress to the code anyway. The couple are planning around the reception.

The usual mistake is a dark suit with a black necktie. That is a business suit, not black tie. If you will wear a tuxedo only once or twice, renting is sensible. Book ahead so there is time to alter the trousers and sleeves. The black tie attire guide covers the code for both men and women in more detail.

contentSections.heading: Black tie optional, and plain "formal"
contentSections.content:
"Optional" relaxes black tie by one step. Emily Post: men may wear a tuxedo, or a dark suit with a white dress shirt, a conservative tie, leather dress shoes and dark socks. Both are correct. Hosts who write "black tie optional" usually expect a mix, with many tuxedos and many dark suits. If you own a tuxedo, wear it. If you don't, a well-fitted navy or charcoal suit with a white shirt is fully within the code, and nobody should feel underdressed in it.

"Formal" without the words "black tie" sits in the same zone. The Emily Post Institute's wedding-guest chart gives men a dark suit, conservative shirt and tie for a formal daytime wedding, and for a formal evening wedding a tuxedo (required only if the invitation says "black tie") or a dark suit. In practice: a formal wedding is a dark-suit wedding with a tuxedo option after dark.

In our analysis of 10,700 posts on r/Weddingattireapproval (16 April – 21 October 2026), the split between the two codes shows up clearly. We flagged posts whose title or text mentions a man's outfit or a male partner. Among those flaired "Black/White Tie" (180 posts), the tuxedo is mentioned in 92 and the suit in 50. Among those flaired "Formal" (240 posts), it reverses: the suit in 92, the tuxedo in 54.

contentSections.heading: Semi-formal and cocktail: the dark-suit codes
contentSections.content:
These two codes cover most evening weddings, and for men they are the same outfit. Emily Post files cocktail under semi-formal and lists a dark business suit, an optional matching vest, a dress shirt, a tie, leather dress shoes and dark dress socks. For events after 6 p.m., it says to dress more formally. The wedding-guest chart gives one daytime exception: a blazer with gray flannels and a tie is acceptable at a semiformal daytime wedding.

The edges are where men hesitate. Can the tie go? Only in daylight, or when the hosts say ties are optional. Gray suit at night? Choose navy or charcoal instead. Tuxedo? That is a rung too high. Our cocktail attire for men and semi-formal attire for men guides answer each of these in detail, with day-versus-evening tables.

contentSections.heading: Dressy casual: the jacket stays, the suit goes
contentSections.content:
Dressy casual is the first code where a man does not need a matching suit. Emily Post's list: a seasonal sport coat or blazer with slacks, a dress or casual button-down shirt or a polo, and the tie optional. For a wedding, choose the dressier end of each option, because the guide's lists are written for any event, from networking evenings to nice restaurants. That means a navy or textured blazer, wool or cotton trousers rather than chinos with worn hems, a collared button-down, and leather shoes or loafers.

The common misreading is treating dressy casual as casual with a nicer shirt. The jacket is the point of the code. Without it, the outfit drops a rung. A tie is optional. Wear one to an evening reception or a church ceremony, and skip it at a daytime garden wedding.

contentSections.heading: Casual wedding attire for men
contentSections.content:
Casual is the bottom of the ladder, and at a wedding it still means looking deliberate. Emily Post's casual list, written for any occasion, includes khakis or good jeans, cargo or Bermuda shorts depending on occasion and climate, plain tees, polos, turtlenecks, casual button-downs or sweaters, and loafers, sneakers or sandals. The guide's broader note is to choose nicer casual wear over baggy house clothes. At a wedding, take the top of that list: pressed khakis or chinos, a crisp button-down or a good polo, and loafers or clean leather shoes. Add a light blazer if the evening cools.

Shorts and sandals are on the list, but whether they suit this wedding depends on the venue and the climate, which is how Emily Post phrases it too. They work at a beach or backyard wedding in summer. They look out of place at a restaurant or a house of worship. Jeans are similar. Dark, clean and well-fitted jeans are acceptable at a truly casual wedding, but chinos are rarely the wrong call. The casual wedding guide covers the code in full.

contentSections.heading: Wordings that aren't on the ladder
contentSections.content:
Plenty of invitations use words no etiquette guide defines. Translate them to the nearest rung:
• Beach, tropical or destination: decide the rung from the rest of the wording and the hour, then lighten the fabric. Beach formal is a light-colored suit and tie. Black tie at a beach resort can mean the white dinner jacket. See the men's beach wedding attire guide.
• Festive (common at holiday weddings): Emily Post's festive code is a seasonal sport coat or blazer in a color of your choice, slacks, an open-collar or dress shirt, and a festive or holiday-themed tie.
• Garden or barn: usually dressy casual or semi-formal in practice. Wear the jacket, and choose shoes that can handle grass or gravel.
• Religious ceremony: Emily Post suggests asking whether the couple's religion or culture requires a head covering and whether bare shoulders, arms or open-toed shoes would offend. For men, keep the jacket on during the service.
• No dress code at all: let the time and the venue decide. Emily Post calls the invitation and the time of the wedding your best guide. An evening wedding with no stated code is a dark-suit wedding.

When a wording falls between two rungs, dress for the higher one. Taking off a tie or a jacket later is easy. Adding one you didn't bring is not.

contentSections.heading: Where men get stuck, by the numbers
contentSections.content:
Across the same 10,700 posts, 1,171 (10.9%) mention a man's outfit or a male partner. Most come from the middle of the ladder. Cocktail-or-no-code and formal invitations each produce about 240 men's posts, black or white tie 180, and semi-formal or dressy casual 126. Casual produces just 32, though casual invitations are rare in the dataset overall (250 posts). That matches the advice above. Men rarely need help at the top of the ladder, where a tuxedo or tailcoat is spelled out, or at the bottom, where almost anything neat passes. The hard calls are suit or tux, and tie or no tie, in the middle.

Three rules settle most of them, whatever the wedding dress code for men says:
1. The jacket is set by the code. Tailcoat, tuxedo, dark suit, blazer or none, as in the table at the top of this page.
2. The clock moves you within a code. After 6 p.m., go darker and keep the tie on.
3. When in doubt, go one step up. At a wedding, slightly overdressed is always easier to fix than underdressed.

faqs.question: What should a man wear to a wedding with no dress code?
faqs.answer: Let the time and venue decide. Emily Post calls the invitation and the time of the wedding your best guide. For an evening wedding, wear a dark suit and tie. For a daytime wedding at a relaxed venue, a blazer with dress trousers and an optional tie is enough.

faqs.question: Can a man wear a black suit to a wedding?
faqs.answer: Yes. A black business suit fits the formal, black tie optional, semi-formal and cocktail codes. It is not a tuxedo, though, so it doesn't meet black tie. Navy or charcoal are often the better choice in daylight, where black can look severe.

faqs.question: Can I wear a tuxedo if the invitation doesn't say black tie?
faqs.answer: At black tie optional and at a formal evening wedding, yes. Emily Post lists the tuxedo as an option for both. At semi-formal, cocktail or anything less formal, no. It is a rung too high, and it can blur you with the groom's party.

serpTop3.weakness: Covers seven codes in about 2,000 words but merges 'Formal or Black Tie Optional' and 'Cocktail or Semiformal' into single entries, has no dressy casual level, cites no source, gives no day/evening split, and says nothing on religious ceremonies or the warm-weather white dinner jacket.

Returned HTTP 403 to every fetcher on 22 Oct 2026 (as recorded in SOURCES.md), so its content could not be verified. #6 blacklapel was assessed instead: six codes, no white tie and no dressy casual, each section ending in an 'Our Recommendation' for its own suit at $599–$1,699, and no etiquette source.
Outfit photos with no dress-code definitions, no garment lists and no guidance on time of day or venue.
